sections.html:
Lincoln County is small, with 8,112 residents, and the county seat, Lincolnton, hosts both tax offices on Humphrey Street. Expect short phone queues. The population was 7,996 in 2010 and 7,690 at the 2020 count, and the July 2025 estimate sits 5.5 percent over the 2020 base. Land area is 210.38 square miles, about 36.6 people per square mile.

Owners occupy 76.6 percent of the 4,779 housing units, and the middle owned home is worth $165,900. Residents past 65 make up 28.1 percent of the county, and 93.9 percent of people kept the same address for a year. Builders took only 55 permits in 2025. A house that a parent or grandparent held for decades comes with a long record, and the buyer will ask for the exemption and tax history in writing.

Median monthly costs for 2020 to 2024 are $1,597 for a mortgage holder, $500 for a paid-off owner and $786 for a renter, and median household income is $56,907.

The one-way drive to work averages 31.2 minutes, which is long and narrows the buyer pool. A seller who prices with that in mind and hands over a clear tax record will see fewer stalled deals. Retail and lodging activity is small, so most buyers are people who already live nearby or work elsewhere.

Humphrey Street holds both. The commissioner works from the courthouse address and the assessors from the county government office.

Lincoln County property tax offices
OfficeAddressPhoneOpen
Tax Commissioner210 Humphrey Street, Lincolnton 30817 (P.O. Box 946)706-359-5536Weekdays, 8 to 4:45
Board of Tax Assessors182 Humphrey Street, Lincolnton 30817 (P.O. Box 340)706-359-5502Weekdays, 8 to 5

The Board of Tax Assessors values every Lincoln County parcel, and its page links to the qPublic property search on its assessors' page. Board meetings are the third Tuesday of each month at 5:30 p.m. in the courthouse conference room, with any change posted on the courthouse bulletin board and the assessors' front door.

You may pay at the window, by post or online. Cash, personal and cashier's checks, money orders and the four major card brands are accepted. Make paper instruments out to the Lincoln County Tax Commissioner.

  • The county adds 3 percent to each card or online payment, so ask the office whether any fee applies to cash, checks or money orders.
  • The mailing address is P.O. Box 946, Lincolnton, GA 30817.

The state sets December 20 unless the county picks something earlier or splits the bill into installments, so read the date on your own bill. Interest does not start until 60 days after the postmark. Pay early if you can, because a late balance complicates a sale.

An appeal is a written letter to the assessors, postmarked within 45 days of the date the notice was mailed. Three paths exist under state law: the Board of Equalization, a hearing officer and an arbitrator, and the Department of Revenue cannot overrule any of them on one parcel.

If the Lincoln assessors have a written policy on electronic service, an appeal may be emailed. Ask at 706-359-5502. Returns of property go to the county tax office from January 1 to April 1. Skip a year and you are treated as having filed last year's figure again. Keep the notice itself, because it states how to file.

The deadline to file for homestead is April 1 of the first year you want relief, and skipping it counts as a waiver. Ask the commissioner whether Lincoln has any local amount above the state's.

  • Refunds: a written claim for tax assessed in error must begin within three years of payment, and an appeal win triggers a refund automatically.
  • Mobile homes: the commissioner issues the location permit, requested within 30 days of placement.

City tax is separate. A city clerk bills it unless the city and county have agreed to one combined bill, so ask which applies.

Make sure this year's bill is paid and hand the proof to the buyer. Whoever owns the house on January 1 owes the entire year, and a sale in midsummer brings no part-year refund.

  • Call 706-359-5536 for any open balance.
  • Tell the buyer your exemption does not carry over.
  • Ask the closing attorney whether a city bill exists beside the county bill.

With over a quarter of residents past 65, many Lincoln sellers hold an age-based exemption, and the buyer applies separately.

sections.h2: Look up your parcel before listing
sections.html:
A qPublic link on the assessors' page opens online property records, and the office at 182 Humphrey Street takes calls at 706-359-5502 if you would rather ask. Read the record before you list, so nothing in it comes as a surprise to you or the buyer.

Check three things on the card: the acreage, the building description and the owner of record. If any looks wrong, call the same number.

A buyer's attorney will ask for a handful of papers. Keep them together and the closing goes faster.

  • The latest tax bill and proof it was paid, from the commissioner on Humphrey Street.
  • Your last assessment notice and any appeal paperwork.
  • Proof of your exemption, if you hold one, so the buyer knows what ends at closing.
  • The deed for the parcel.
  • Any mobile home location permit, if a manufactured home sits on the land.

Builders took out only 55 permits in 2025, so a ready file can set your listing apart from other homes on the market. A cash buyer can skip lender appraisal and repair requests, but the payoff and the recorded deed still happen.

sections.h2: A step by step timeline for a Lincoln County sale
sections.html:
Selling a house in a small county moves best when you work through the offices in order. Start in January through April if you can, because that is the window for returns and homestead filings, and the assessors will have time to answer questions.

  1. Call the Board of Tax Assessors at 706-359-5502 and confirm the acreage, building description, exemption status and owner of record on the parcel card.
  2. Call the Tax Commissioner at 706-359-5536 and ask whether the year's bill is out, whether it is paid, and what any open balance is.
  3. Find out if the city also bills the property. A city clerk bills separately unless city and county agreed to one combined bill.
  4. List the house, and give your buyer's attorney the folder of papers described above.
  5. At closing, have the attorney pay any open balance from your proceeds and divide the year's tax between you and the buyer.
  6. Tell the buyer to file a new homestead application by April 1, because yours ends with your ownership.

Georgia gives no part-year refund, so the contract is the only place the split can be settled. If the house came to you through a family estate, the buyer will want the tax and exemption history in writing, and an organized record will keep the deal from stalling.

faqs.q: When can I visit the Lincolnton tax office?
faqs.a: Weekdays from 8 to 4:45 at 210 Humphrey Street.

faqs.q: Is there a surcharge on Lincoln card payments?
faqs.a: Yes, 3 percent on card and online payments.

faqs.q: What is the cutoff for a Lincoln appeal?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the mailing date on the notice, judged by postmark.

faqs.q: Which day do Lincoln bills come due?
faqs.a: December 20 by default, unless the county sets another date. Your bill states it.

faqs.q: Can I get back tax I overpaid in Lincoln County?
faqs.a: Possibly. A written claim has to begin within three years of paying.
